Since there are interdependencies between these four draft guidances in conducting a well- controlled RWE study program, we believe it is important to evaluate the series of guidances in their totality.

EMD Serono believes that the FDA should consider how RWD can be standardized and used across similar databases etc. We encourage that FDA leverage prior knowledge and cross-reference familiar data sets, study designs, and analytical methods.
We recommend that FDA considers endorsing the existing STaRT-RWE structured template for planning and reporting on the implementation of real world evidence (RWE) studies.
We recommend that FDA expand the scope of the guidance beyond approved drugs and biological products but rather as part of the totality of evidence for the application

the content of the guidance fits other type of data sources such as registries (e.g., national and quality registries from Nordic countries that are widely used for regulatory studies) and EMD Serono recommends that FDA explicitly describe this in the guidance or in one of the other planned draft guidances.
Furthermore, we suggest that the FDA considers leveraging the estimand framework to articulate the guidance in reference to existing ICH guidance4.
Lastly, we recommend that the guidance also includes clarity on the elements out of scope.
EMD Serono suggests that FDA develop a flow schematic layout sequence of activities, including inviting sponsors to seek FDA input.
In addition, we recommend that the flow schematic layout also describes whether the FDA expects the document to be submitted in draft version or final version.

We suggest that it would be helpful to identify streamlined and efficient FDA-sponsor communication methods to facilitate rapid RWD/RWE generation that goes beyond the RWE Pilot Program for those sponsors not being part of the pilot program.

We suggest that FDA provide further clarity on the sufficiency of the data used to support the intended use and when the data are adequate for the intended use while at the same time allowing flexibility based on the regulatory context.

EMD Serono would find it helpful if FDA would provide more dedicated recommendations according to the regulatory context (eg. to the intended use of RWE as substantial or supportive evidence, or description of unmet need or population).

We would recommend, for the final protocol, to refer to “after approval by IRB” and for the SAP, to “before conducting the analysis” when the operational plan requires time between the protocol approval and actual data analysis.

The guidance would greatly benefit from inclusion of additional detail regarding such meeting opportunities, including how sponsors may engage as appropriate (e.g., review divisions in addition to the FDA Real-World Evidence Subcommittee), meeting type and associated timelines.

Janssen encourages FDA to consider revisions to the guidance that allow for a more feasible approach to a series of focused meetings between FDA and sponsors that allows for review and feedback at milestones for designing, conducting, and reporting fit- for-purpose RWE.
For example, FDA could consider mechanisms that allow individual sponsors to use prior validation of the same or similar endpoints
as well as the potential to share across stakeholders collated information on validated endpoints.

Janssen also requests that FDA outline some of the challenges associated with determining negative predictive value (an exercise that would require extensive sampling and validation of ‘non-cases’) as well as potential solutions as the guidance is finalized.
Janssen requests that FDA specifically indicate in the guidance that RWD may be effectively leveraged as external control arms.

Janssen recommends that FDA allow for the use of other platforms (e.g., Structured Template and Reporting Tool for Real World Evidence (STaRT-RWE)) beyond ct.gov that were designed and more suitable for registration of RWD studies.

Janssen requests that FDA explicitly acknowledge this point in the guidance and discuss alternatives for providing such information to FDA, if the sponsor is not able to provide the RWD directly to FDA.

To this end, we encourage FDA to adopt a flexible approach by developing and outlining in guidance “best practices” that can be leveraged across various RWD analysis methods and that allow for flexibility in the future.
Janssen would also welcome FDA to make publicly available non-proprietary lessons learned for RWD study designs and methods to support shared learnings across industry.

We encourage FDA to recognize sponsors may need to work with the provider of the data source technology, particularly to support discussions related to the “data accrual, curation, and transformation into the final study-specific dataset.”

Further, where the FDA suggests modifications to EHRs may be necessary to collect extensive additional information to support prospective clinical studies (line 152), we encourage cooperation among all stakeholders to consider the value and associated processes of collecting additional data that may be useful for clinical care and leveraged for research as well.
We strongly encourage ongoing cooperation and collaboration across government agencies and other stakeholders to support the one-time collection of data that can be used for multiple purposes,

We encourage FDA to engage with various stakeholders, including patients, to consider how this process can be supported by all types of entities, including smaller companies and non-profits, to create data resources that can be used by all stakeholders.

Further, we encourage FDA to act as a convenor of various stakeholders who are evaluating similar questions in obtaining, curating, validating and linking data, to leverage a common effort and reduce continued fragmented approaches toward standardization.

We appreciate that FDA recognizes the value of these data for clinical research purposes, and we encourage FDA to work with government agencies and various stakeholders to break through these barriers.

Future revisions to this guidance document should stress the dynamic nature of this topic and highlight FDA’s flexibility and receptivity in engaging with data providers to creatively explore other concerns, approaches, and considerations specific to drug development programs.

Patient privacy must never be sacrificed at the expense of broader use of EHR data for regulatory decision making. Strong, HIPAA-compliant data security measures must always be in place to ensure the responsible use and disclosure of EHR data for all purposes.
While acknowledging that the sponsor is ultimately accountable, we recommend FDA clarify the role of the data provider (e.g., EHR data curator/vendor) in support of regulatory decision making.

As part of the review of study feasibility, we recommend that sponsors obtain from the data provider evidence of the completeness, accuracy, and plausibility of the data as well as the scientific justification for using data standards.

Recommendation: For community healthcare systems actively involved (or seeking to become involved) in clinical drug trials, we seek specific FDA commentary on addition of the following clinical trial criteria to routine care EHR:
If concerns over continuity of coverage would likely affect clinical readouts, FDA may want to consider emphasizing
Recommendation: (i) FDA consideration of an anonymous “results-based checksum” capable of identifying and eliminating redundant de-identified sources of EMR data.
(ii) FDA consideration of requiring data vendors routinely communicate to recipients of curated data whether the source data came from a single healthcare network or multiple networks.
(i) data vendors continually involve data engineering teams to ensure maximal extraction of unstructured data elements from EHRs,
(ii) human review of all curated data sets prior to use, particularly for data sets created by automated means (e.g., NLP, AI, etc.),
(iii) not relying only on standard data export formats (e.g., FHIR, HL7, etc.) that often lack important clinical metadata (e.g., physician notes),

(iv) clinical protocols should specify the assumptions and parameters of the computer algorithms used, the data source from which the information was used to build the algorithm, whether the algorithm was supervised (i.e., using input and review by experts) or unsupervised, and the metrics associated with validation of the methods,
(v) FDA reviewable QA/QC validation reports from data vendors who employ automated software means of data curation

Recommendation: FDA provide more accurate definitions for otherwise vague routine clinical care terminology (e.g., more precisely define “date of diagnosis” as date of pathology lab diagnosis / date of clinical lab values diagnosis / date patient was informed of diagnosis).
Recommendation: FDA work with stakeholders on improving propensity score matching by identifying key RWD covariates.
Data vendors should display full transparency by providing the entire patient cohort and describing how final patient cohorts were selected in an unbiased fashion.

To best maintain data integrity, instead of deleting or “correcting” seemingly improbable values, GRN recommends documenting and flagging suspicious data in need of further review and confirmation by sponsors.

Recommendation: Parties who use and disclose identifiable EHR data for regulatory decision- making purposes should be legally bound to HIPAA regulations via Business Associate Agreements / Data Use Agreements.

Recommendation: Data providers should: (i) establish policies and procedures for developing and testing the de-identification process, and (ii) routinely create validation reports prior to electronic transmission to third-party end users.
GRN recommends the use of a dedicated, HIPAA compliant clinical operations group to oversee QA/QC issues.

GRN agrees that all manual and automated data retrieval and transformation processes should be thoroughly assessed from data collection through writing of the final study report to ensure data integrity.

As FDA continues to develop its Real World Evidence (RWE) Program and explores ways to use data to inform its regulatory decision-making, FDA should consider the role clearinghouses could play given their ability to aggregate data and link patients across data sets.
